words.definition: a tax imposed on goods imported from or exported to another country
words.example: The government raised tariffs on imported steel.

words.definition: the amount by which spending exceeds income or exports fall short of imports
words.example: The country's trade deficit widened significantly last year.

words.definition: an amount left over after all requirements have been met
words.example: The nation recorded a trade surplus for the first time in years.

words.definition: a general and sustained rise in prices, reducing purchasing power
words.example: Rising inflation has made everyday goods more expensive.

words.definition: a period of temporary economic decline during which trade and activity slow
words.example: The economy fell into recession after years of steady growth.

words.definition: to support an industry or activity financially, typically with government funds
words.example: The government decided to subsidize renewable energy producers.

words.definition: a raw material or primary product that can be bought and sold
words.example: Oil remains one of the world's most traded commodities.

words.definition: to rise and fall irregularly in level or amount
words.example: Currency exchange rates fluctuate constantly throughout the day.

words.definition: strict economic policies imposed by a government to reduce spending
words.example: The government introduced austerity measures to cut public debt.

words.definition: the practice of shielding domestic industries from foreign competition through tariffs or restrictions
words.example: Rising protectionism has slowed the growth of global trade.

words.definition: to remove or relax government restrictions on economic activity
words.example: The country began to liberalize its markets in the 1990s.

words.definition: the state of relying heavily on something or someone else
words.example: Many developing economies suffer from a dependency on a single export.

words.definition: power or influence used to achieve a desired outcome
words.example: Larger economies have significant leverage in trade negotiations.

words.definition: to make a problem, conflict, or situation worse
words.example: New tariffs could exacerbate tensions between the two countries.

words.definition: something intended to encourage economic activity or growth
words.example: The government approved a large stimulus package to boost spending.

words.definition: an official ban on trade or other commercial activity with a particular country
words.example: The United Nations imposed an embargo on the country's exports.

words.definition: fair and impartial, especially in the distribution of resources
words.example: Negotiators called for a more equitable global trade system.

words.definition: a great difference or inequality between two things
words.example: The disparity between rich and poor nations continues to grow.

words.definition: to make the severity of a problem or its effects less serious
words.example: Trade agreements can help mitigate the impact of economic shocks.

words.definition: likely to change rapidly and unpredictably
words.example: Global markets have grown increasingly volatile in recent months.

text: Global trade has never been simple, but rarely has it seemed as volatile as it does today. When one nation imposes a tariff on imported goods, trading partners frequently retaliate, triggering a cycle of protectionism that can exacerbate tensions built over decades of liberalized commerce. Commodity prices fluctuate wildly in response, leaving smaller economies, often already burdened by trade deficits, especially vulnerable. Some governments respond with austerity, cutting spending to narrow a widening deficit; others prefer a stimulus package, hoping to subsidize struggling industries back to health. Neither approach is without risk: austerity can deepen a recession, while excessive stimulus may fuel inflation. Wealthier nations, wielding considerable leverage over international markets, can weather an embargo or a sudden downturn far more easily than developing countries whose economies remain dependent on a handful of exports. This dependency, critics argue, perpetuates a disparity between rich and poor that no amount of surplus generated by trade alone can mitigate. For global commerce to become genuinely equitable, negotiators must look beyond short-term national advantage and consider, however reluctantly, the interconnected fate of every economy involved.

questions.question: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: Global trade is entirely stable and predictable.
Global trade is increasingly volatile, and addressing inequality between nations requires cooperation.
Only wealthy nations are affected by trade disputes.
Tariffs always benefit the countries that impose them.

questions.question: According to the passage, what risk does austerity carry?
options: It can deepen a recession.
It always causes inflation.
It eliminates trade deficits instantly.
It has no economic consequences.

questions.question: What can be inferred about developing countries dependent on a few exports?
options: They are generally unaffected by fluctuating commodity prices.
They are especially vulnerable to global economic instability.
They have more leverage than wealthier nations.
They benefit most from protectionism.

questions.question: What does the passage say wealthier nations can withstand more easily than developing countries?
options: An embargo or sudden economic downturn
A rise in domestic inflation only
A decrease in commodity prices only
A change in government leadership

questions.question: What is the author's purpose in the final sentence of the passage?
options: To argue that national self-interest should always come first
To call for greater international cooperation for a fairer trade system
To dismiss the idea of global economic interdependence
To criticize wealthy nations for having any leverage at all

questions.question: In the passage, 'exacerbate' is closest in meaning to:
options: Resolve
Worsen
Ignore
Measure
